levelIntro.cloud-manual: Traffic surges to ×10! Keep 3 servers (computers running your app) alive: Boost busy ones, Restart crashed ones, Roll back bad updates. Good luck!
levelIntro.cloud-configure: Now let Kubernetes do the work. Pick your settings and keep the cost under budget.
levelIntro.cloud-replay: Same storm, new setup. Sit back and watch Kubernetes handle it. You can still tap Restart or Roll back if needed.

tutorialHint: Tap Boost on the busiest server. Tap Restart the moment one crashes.

manual.badDeploy: Bad update! Half your users are getting errors.
manual.crashToast: Server {n} crashed! Tap Restart to bring it back.
manual.deployToast: A bad update went out. Tap Roll back!
manual.paused: Paused. Tap Resume when you're ready.
manual.faultToast: Server {n}'s hardware failed! Tap Restart to bring it back.

configure.heading: Set up Kubernetes
configure.loadBalancerHelp: Spreads users evenly across your pods, so no single pod gets swamped.
configure.podsHelp: Min: pods always running, even when quiet. Max: the most allowed at peak.
configure.thresholdHelp: Lower means pods get added sooner. New pods take 4 seconds to start.
configure.selfHealingHelp: Kubernetes restarts crashed pods by itself, in about 3 seconds.
configure.rollingHelp: Tries new updates on one pod first. Bad ones roll back automatically.
configure.overBudget: Over budget. Fewer pods will cost less.

replay.healed: A pod crashed. Kubernetes replaced it.
replay.scaledUp: Getting busy. The autoscaler is adding pods.
replay.scaledDown: Quieter now. The autoscaler removed a pod.
replay.autoRollback: Bad update caught on one pod and rolled back automatically.
replay.podCrashed: Pod {n} crashed! Tap Restart to bring it back.
replay.podsSummary: Pods: {start} at the start, {peak} at the peak.
replay.stormOver: Storm over. By hand {manual}%, with Kubernetes {auto}%.
replay.crashes: {n} pods crashed. Tap Restart to bring them back.
replay.faultHealed: Pod {n}'s machine died. Kubernetes restarted it automatically.
replay.faultNoHeal: Pod {n}'s machine died. Without self-healing, it waits for a human.

diagnosis.perfect: Spot on! Your pods handled the whole storm, and you stayed under budget.
diagnosis.overBudget: Rock solid, but pricey: too many pods blew the budget. Lower Min pods and let the autoscaler add more.
diagnosis.tooFewPods: Max pods was too low for the peak, so your pods got overloaded and crashed. Raise Max pods.
diagnosis.thresholdHigh: New pods arrived too late. They take 4 seconds to start, so set a lower busy level.
diagnosis.noLoadBalancer: Without a load balancer, one pod got swamped while others sat quiet. Turn it on to spread users evenly.
diagnosis.noHealing: A pod died and kept getting users for 15 seconds. Self-healing restarts it in about 3.
diagnosis.noRolling: The bad update hit every pod at once. Turn on rolling updates to test it on one pod first.
diagnosis.overBudgetShaky: Too pricey and still wobbly. Pick a sensible busy level and fewer Max pods, not more pods everywhere.
diagnosis.overBudgetMinOne: Over budget: pods get added too eagerly. Raise the busy level a little, or lower Max pods.

hint: Turn on all three switches. Keep Min pods low, allow enough Max pods, and add pods at around 60–70% busy.
timeUp: Time's up! Let's see how it held up.

result.heading3: Unshakeable! Nothing kept your app down.
result.heading0: Storms are tough. Have another go!

learned: By hand you kept {manual}% uptime; Kubernetes kept {auto}%. Tapping can't keep up, but automation can, at a cost.
